title: Calibrating a syringe pump by gravimetry
content:
A syringe pump computes plunger speed from the syringe inner diameter you program. Real syringes — 3D-printed or commercial — have diameter tolerance, so the delivered flow can be off by several percent even if the pump moves perfectly. In our tests a "3 mL" syringe with a nominal 8.94 mm bore actually delivered +2.5 %; the corrected diameter was 9.05 mm. Delivered flow = drive-head speed × syringe cross-section, so there are two error sources: the syringe diameter (below) and the pump mechanics (how far the plunger really travels). Gravimetry alone can't tell them apart. On a trustworthy pump (e.g. Harvard PHD 2000) the diameter correction below is enough; on a home-built pump calibrate the mechanics too — see Two errors in one. This gravimetric calibration needs only an analytical balance — no flow sensor. Water weighs ~1 g/mL, so 1 mg ≈ 1 µL: the balance gives real dispensed volume directly. 
Q_real = mass / (ρ_water · time)
D_real = D₀ · √(Q_real / Q_set)
If the balance reads more flow than programmed → the syringe is wider than you told the pump → increase the diameter. Enter D_real and the pump delivers true flow. The calculator calibrate.py does the math — you just type the numbers you measured. Equipment Analytical balance, 1 mg (0.001 g); 0.1 mg is even better. Syringe under test, filled with bubble-free distilled water. Parafilm + a small receiving tube (e.g. Eppendorf). Tweezers/tongs for handling calibration weights (skin oil weighs enough to matter). The syringe pump (this project). For the pump-mechanics check (optional, see below): a dial indicator or digital caliper (0.01 mm) to measure drive-head travel. Step 0 — Calibrate the balance (once) Place it on a stable, level table (centre the bubble with the feet); no drafts, sun or vibration. Warm it up for ≥ 1 hour powered on. Empty pan, reading 0.0. Enter external calibration (on CGOLDENWALL/JoanLab HZ-type balances: Set → menu → e-cal; it requests a standard weight, e.g. cal-200 = 200 g). Place the exact standard weight with tongs, wait, remove when prompted → returns to 0.0. Verify: place a known weight (e.g. 100 g) and check it reads correctly. Step 1 — Prepare the run Fill the syringe, purge all air (a single bubble ruins a run). Mount it in the pump. Program the nominal diameter D₀ (caliper the inner bore, or use the syringe spec) and the target flow Q_set. Let the pump drip into any waste tube until the flow is steady — we use 5 min; the first minutes clear residual bubbles and let the mechanics settle. Step 2 — Collect the output, weighed (timed collection) Prepare the collection tube first: close the empty Eppendorf, seal the top with parafilm, pierce a small hole with the sharp tip of scissors (just big enough for the capillary — keeps evaporation low), and stand it on a small, very light base (we cut one from the foam used to pack boxes — negligible mass, keeps the round-bottom tube upright on the pan). Weigh it in this final state (tube + parafilm + hole + foam base) → m_empty, or tare to zero. Then collect, without stopping the flow: with the flow already steady (Step 1), move the capillary from the waste tube into the collection tube through the parafilm hole, and start the stopwatch at that instant. Collect for an exactly timed interval t (t goes straight into the result). Move the capillary out, press the parafilm closed over the hole, and weigh immediately → m_full. Δm = m_full − m_empty.

1 — Caliper the bore to get the nominal diameter D₀
2 — Seal the tube top with parafilm
3 — Pierce a small hole with a scissor tip
4 — Insert the capillary through the hole
Aim for Δm ≥ 100 mg (e.g. 10 min at 1000 µL/h ≈ 167 mg → <1 % uncertainty at 1 mg). Step 3 — Compute and correct ➡️ Open the web calculator — type the weighed values, get the corrected diameter (no install). 
python3 calibrate.py --d0 8.94 --qset 1000 --mass 170.5 --minutes 10 --temp 20
#   flow real (balance): 1024.8 uL/h  (+2.5 %)
#   CORRECTED DIAMETER : 9.05 mm   <- enter this on the pump
Enter D_real on the pump. Repeat one point to confirm Q_real ≈ Q_set. Step 4 — Verify linearity Repeat at 2–3 flows (e.g. 500 / 1000 / 2000 µL/h) with the corrected diameter. If they all give the same D_real, the calibration is solid and flow-independent. Two errors in one: syringe diameter vs. pump mechanics Gravimetry measures the delivered volume — the end-to-end truth. But that number lumps two physically independent error sources together (EURAMET CG-27; IEC 60601-2-24): 
delivered flow  =  drive-head speed   ×   syringe cross-section area
                   └─ pump mechanics ─┘    └── syringe geometry ──┘
Syringe geometry (the diameter): bore tolerance is 1 % (large syringes) to 3 % (small). Scales flow by a constant factor, independent of flow rate and of position along the barrel. Pump mechanics (how far the plunger actually travels per command): lead-screw pitch, steps/mm, microstep linearity, coupling backlash/compliance. Commercial drivers spec ±1–2 %. The diameter-only calibration above (Steps 1–4) folds both into an effective diameter. That is fine when the pump mechanics are trustworthy — e.g. a Harvard PHD 2000 (±0.35 %). For a home-built pump (stepper + lead screw) you cannot assume that: a steps/mm error disguises itself as a diameter error, and gravimetry alone cannot tell them apart (both scale flow by the same constant factor). How the pump is calibrated in the literature Most open-hardware pump papers do not measure the plunger travel directly — they compute the step size from geometry and finish with an end-to-end gravimetric calibration that folds mechanics and geometry into a single constant: Geometric starting point — steps (or microsteps) per unit volume follow from the drivetrain: µsteps/µL = (steps_per_rev × microstepping) / (π · (ID/2)² · lead) e.g. a Marlin pump with 200 steps/rev, 16 µsteps, an 8 mm/rev screw and a BD 10 mL syringe (ID 14.5 mm) → 2.42 µstep/µL, set in firmware with M92 E2.42 (Baden et al., 2024). Gravimetric finish — Wijnen, Hunt, Anzalone & Pearce (Open-Source Syringe Pump Library, PLoS ONE 2014): set the calibration to a nominal value, dispense a volume twice, weigh the second push, divide actual / commanded, enter the ratio, repeat 3×. One number now captures the whole chain. The catch — and the whole point of this section — is that this does not separate the two errors. A lead-screw whose real pitch differs from nominal is indistinguishable from a wrong bore, so it is silently absorbed into an effective, per-pump inner diameter (several 3D-printed-pump studies report using a device-specific ID for each pump for exactly this reason). That is fine if you only want accurate flow. It is not fine if you want to know which part is off — for that you must measure the travel on its own. Separating the two — the "displacement method" EURAMET CG-27 §4.3.3 names this the displacement method: mount a mirror on the pusher block and measure its travelled distance directly, independent of the syringe — Q = (x₂−x₁)/Δt · πr² — which captures the "unloaded movement of the syringe driver head" (Batista et al., 2020 [1]). The lab-grade version uses a laser interferometer (nanometre resolution); the workshop version is the same measurand with a dial indicator / caliper (~0.01 mm) — the familiar 3D-printer axis steps/mm calibration applied to the pump carriage (Method A). If you have a reference pump instead of a dial indicator, Method B gets you there without disassembly. Caveat (from the same guide). The displacement method measures the unloaded travel. With a real syringe, rubber-stopper compression and drivetrain compliance add a further error the travel alone cannot see. So the full picture is travel (mechanics) + gravimetry (loaded, real syringe): the gap between them is the stopper/compliance contribution. Method A — Measure plunger travel directly (no syringe) This checks the mechanics on their own: does the drive head move the distance you command? Mount a dial indicator (or digital caliper) against the drive head / carriage and zero it. Remove the syringe or leave it empty — this test is purely mechanical. Command a long move of known length L_set (e.g. 20.00 mm). Long travel makes the reading error (±0.01–0.02 mm) a negligible fraction. Read the actual travel L_real off the indicator. Mechanical error = L_real / L_set − 1. Correct it (inverse): - Firmware with a steps/mm constant → steps_per_mm_corr = steps_per_mm × (L_real / L_set). - Repeat over the full stroke (0→20, 20→40 mm …) to catch lead-screw non-uniformity. (Optional) Backlash: command a move, then reverse; the dead distance before the indicator starts moving is the backlash. Only matters if you ever reverse — infusion-only runs don't. After this the pump delivers the commanded distance. Any gravimetric error that remains is then genuinely the syringe diameter, which you fix with Steps 1–4. Method B — Cross-check against a reference pump (same syringe) If you have a trustworthy reference pump (Harvard PHD 2000) you can split the error without a dial indicator, because the syringe geometry is common to both pumps and cancels: Run the same syringe on the reference pump, gravimetric → error ε_ref ≈ syringe geometry (reference mechanics are ±0.35 %). Run the same syringe on the pump under test, same Q_set, gravimetric → error ε_total. Pump-mechanics error ≈ ε_total − ε_ref. Method A is absolute and needs only a caliper; Method B needs a reference pump but no disassembly. Use A to calibrate a new pump build, B to audit a pump already in service. Order of operations First calibrate the mechanics (Method A) → the pump moves the true distance. Then calibrate the diameter (Steps 1–4) → the flow is true. In this order the diameter you end up with is the real bore, not a number that silently absorbs a steps/mm error. Mechanism cycle. On a lead-screw pump the delivered flow carries a slow periodic ripple at the screw's revolution period ("mechanism cycle time", EURAMET CG-27). Time each gravimetric collection over ≥ 2 full revolutions of the screw to average it out. This ripple is expected — it is not a leak or a bubble. Practical tips (what ruins a run) Evaporation: at 1000 µL/h an open tube loses ~1 mg/min — always parafilm, and weigh immediately after capping. Weights with tongs, never fingers. Exclude the first ~5 min of each run (stabilization + bubble clearing). Record water temperature; the tool adjusts density (20 °C → 0.99821 g/mL). ±2 °C is negligible (<0.1 %). Bubbles: purge before, and if the output suddenly spikes/dips erratically, there is air in the line — stop and purge. Optional: cross-check with a flow sensor (higher precision) The balance fixes the diameter. If you also have an in-line flow sensor, the same runs let you check — and calibrate — the sensor against the balance (ground truth), and then use the sensor as a continuous flow reference without weighing every time. calibrate.py reports the sensor factor if you pass --sensor-ulh <reading>. For the flow-sensor hardware, firmware and high-rate acquisition, see the Rio controller: ➡️ wenzel-lab/rio-controller (pressure/flow module). EURAMET is the European Association of National Metrology Institutes — the body that defines SI-traceable measurement in Europe. IPQ (Instituto Português da Qualidade) is Portugal's national metrology institute; Elsa Batista (IPQ) leads both the guide and the displacement-method papers above.
